newsitem.title: USA: California approves sweeping tax reform measure.
newsitem.headline: California approves sweeping tax reform measure.

text.p: Californian voters on Tuesday approved an initiative that would require all local taxes to be submitted to voters for approval despite warnings that the measure would undermine local government finances.
With nearly 70 percent of precincts reporting, Proposition 218 had the support of 56.5 percent of voetrs while 43.5 percent were opposed, state election officials said.

The measure would make it more difficult for counties and other local governments to raise fees, assessments and taxes. Already at the bottom of the political food chain, Californian counties and other local governments could lose precious revenues and be forced to slash services, opponents warned.

Known as the Right to Vote on Taxes Act, proposition 218 has shaken elected officials in California and municipal analysts on Wall Street. The California Society of Municipal Analysts has warned that the tax measure could have negative credit implications for some local government bond issues.
Jonathan Coupal, who helped to draft Proposition 218 for the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, said bond firms were exaggerating the measure's negative implications.
"The world won't come to an end. It won't," said Coupal, who is director of legal affairs for the association.
Proposition 218 was designed to close loopholes in California's Proposition 13, which was also spearheaded by activists with the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association.

The passage in 1978 of Proposition 13 in California rolled back local property taxes and drastically curtailed the ability of counties to raise revenues to cover expenses. Proposition 13 also set off a wave of tax reduction efforts across the country.

Proposition 218, which would apply to all cities, counties, special districts, redevelopment agencies and school districts in the state, would strengthen existing law to require that all new local taxes be submitted to voters for approval. It would also allow property owners to approve new assessments and strictly limit the use of fees and charges.

The non-partisan California legislative analyst estimated that the measure would reduce local revenues by about $100 million per year. Opponents of the tax measure insist the reduction would be significantly greater.
